title: Google Sends Four AI Chips Into Orbit as Project Suncatcher's First Test Takes Flight
excerpt: A Planet-built prototype carrying four Trillium TPUs launched October 1 on SpaceX's Transporter-18 — the first step in Google's research into whether AI can run in space.
body:
• Google has put four of its AI accelerator chips into orbit aboard a refrigerator-sized prototype satellite built with Earth-imaging company Planet.
  • The satellite, internally called MVP, launched October 1 aboard SpaceX's Transporter-18 rideshare mission from Vandenberg Space Force Base — one of 130 payloads on the Falcon 9.
  • The four Trillium-generation TPUs will run Google's Gemma model in 15-minute bursts, testing whether the chips survive launch, radiation and the thermal extremes of orbit.
  • Google says a future two-satellite test is planned for 2027 — but estimates SpaceX's Starship would need ~1,600 launches before orbital data centers become economically viable.

Google's artificial intelligence chips have left the building — literally. On October 1, a prototype satellite carrying four of Google's Tensor Processing Units lifted off aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 from Vandenberg Space Force Base in California, marking the first time the company's custom AI hardware has operated in orbit. The launch is the first hardware step in Project Suncatcher, Google's long-horizon research programme into whether machine learning infrastructure could one day run in space.

"Our team has confirmed contact with the satellite and it is operating as expected."

— Travis Beals, senior director of Paradigms of Intelligence, Google

What actually launched

The satellite — internally called MVP, for minimum viable prototype — was built by Planet on a standard satellite platform and rides on SpaceX's Transporter-18 rideshare mission, which carried 130 payloads into a dawn-dusk sun-synchronous orbit roughly 400 miles above Earth. Google confirmed first contact with MVP the same evening.

The cargo is four Trillium-generation TPUs — the same class of chip Google uses in its Earth-bound data centers. Over the coming weeks, Google will gather data on how the chips cope with the physical stress of launch, cosmic radiation and the thermal extremes of orbit. As Techtimes reported, Google simultaneously published a peer-reviewed paper in the journal Joule laying out the research behind the mission.

The real test: heat, not radiation

Pre-launch coverage focused heavily on whether the chips would survive radiation — and ground tests were reassuring. Google's Trillium TPUs survived a radiation dose greater than they would receive on a five-year space mission at UC Davis's Crocker Nuclear Laboratory. Launch itself is its own problem: Google says components see sustained acceleration up to 10 times the force of gravity, with individual chips facing 50 to 100 g.

But the binding constraint, according to the Joule paper, is thermal management. In a vacuum there is no air to carry heat away, so the chips will run a version of Google's Gemma AI model in 15-minute bursts, shedding heat through heat pipes, pumped-fluid loops and radiators. The mission's central question is whether that cooling design keeps computing hardware within its limits — and the answer will arrive in 15-minute increments over the year-long mission.

Why space at all

Google frames the programme as a response to terrestrial constraints: power availability and cooling are becoming the limiting factors for AI infrastructure growth on Earth, not chips or models. Space offers abundant solar power and a cold environment — but at a forbidding cost. According to TechCrunch's reporting, Google estimates SpaceX's Starship would need to launch roughly 1,600 times before orbital data centers become economically viable. The gap between one prototype satellite and a functioning off-world data center is enormous, and Google is not pretending otherwise: the bigger test comes in 2027, when it plans to fly two satellites together, each eventually carrying dozens of TPUs linked by high-bandwidth lasers.

Context: the orbital-computing race

Google is not alone in looking up. SpaceX itself sees space-based supercomputers as the next step in AI infrastructure, touting "infinite real estate" and a way around the community backlash terrestrial data centers increasingly face over power and water use. For now, Suncatcher's MVP is an experiment, not a deployment — "a very minimal test to make sure the chips can run in space," as Beals told NPR.

What's next

Planet will finish commissioning the satellite's systems before Google begins the TPU tests. If the chips survive their year in orbit and the cooling design holds, the 2027 dual-satellite mission will test the harder problems: dozens of chips, laser interconnects, and whether parallel computing can genuinely work at orbital scale.
